$comment: Single source of truth for the playground: every app listed here exists in apps/<id>/ and is built and shown in the gallery.
`id` is immutable: it is the folder name under apps/, the URL segment, and the key used to derive the GitHub and CLI links.
Build output is assumed to be 'dist'; add "outDir" only when the toolchain differs (e.g. Next.js static export writes to 'out').

apps.name: Starter
apps.description: The smallest setup that still shows what Morphic Blocks is made of: elements, modes and views, with one mount call and five short behaviors.
apps.details:
Each of the five blocks (print, text, number, math and repeat) has five elements: a title, an icon, a one sentence hint, pseudocode and JavaScript. Two modes pick from these elements. The blocks mode serves the toolbox and the workspace: tiles show title, icon, block and hint, while the workspace draws only the mode's first code element, the plain word pseudocode. The javascript mode fills the code view, which is editable by structure.

A small ⓘ button next to each pane names the mode it shows. Run executes the program and shows what it printed. Copy this app to start your own project.
apps.question: What is Morphic Blocks made of?

apps.name: Embed Anywhere
apps.description: A friendly tutorial article about loops with three small block editors placed between its paragraphs, each one the same reusable web component with a live Python preview and a Run button.
apps.details:
The page reads like an ordinary blog post. Between the paragraphs sit three figures, one per step: repeat a fixed number of times, count with a variable, and repeat while a condition holds. Each figure has its own tray of blocks, a workspace, a live Python preview and a small output area. It opens with a starter program whose output is already shown, and Run refreshes the output after the reader changes the blocks.

All three are the same <morphic-editor> custom element, built with Lit and configured only by attributes: which blocks its toolbox offers, which program it starts with, its height and its caption. Each instance runs its own Morphic Blocks engine, so the editors stay fully independent, and the tag could be dropped into a CMS, a wiki or a learning platform just like an image. Behaviors turn the blocks into JavaScript with the same meaning as the Python shown, and a loop that never ends is stopped after a thousand rounds.
apps.question: Can I put it into any page?

apps.name: Block to Text
apps.description: One Python program moves step by step from plain word blocks to Python blocks to Python text, and Run shows what it prints.
apps.details:
Nine blocks (print, text, number, math, compare, if, repeat and a variable set and get pair) in two modes: plain words such as "repeat 3 times" and Python. Three presets are the steps: plain word blocks; plain word blocks next to the same program as Python blocks, which come from a second, read only engine that copies the program after every change; and Python blocks next to Python text that can be edited by structure.

Every step has an Output area with a Run button. A behaviors file turns each block into JavaScript that does what its Python does, so the output matches what Python would print, and loops stop after 1,000 rounds.
apps.question: How do learners move from blocks to text?

apps.name: Turtle Drawing
apps.description: Picture blocks with no words steer a turtle that draws on a big canvas, so even children who cannot read yet can program a drawing.
apps.details:
Five blocks show only a picture and a number or a color: forward, turn left, turn right, pen color and repeat. The toolbox is a set of big colored tiles to drag onto the workspace, and both float above the drawing paper. The workspace starts with a square, and the drawing can be dragged and zoomed.

Run turns the blocks into JavaScript that calls a turtle (turtle.forward(100), turtle.right(90) and so on). The app runs that code with its own turtle, which writes down every move, and then plays the moves back step by step on the canvas. Children never see code: a small </> button shows parents and teachers the same program in Logo (pen blue, repeat 4 [ forward 100 right 90 ]) in a read only preview view. A program that loops more than 1,000 rounds is stopped with a short message.
apps.question: Can blocks drive something else, like a drawing?

apps.name: Side by Side
apps.description: Programs are built entirely in text, with no blocks on screen, and the same program can be read side by side in Go, C++, Java, Python and JavaScript.
apps.details:
Blockly runs hidden and holds the program; people only see and edit text. Snippets from the toolbox are dragged into the code on the left, and values, names and types are changed by clicking them. Each of the two text views has its own language dropdown, and the snippets follow the language on the left.

Sixteen blocks cover printing, values, math, comparisons, variables, if and else, loops and functions. A single type dropdown (number, text, true/false) turns into int, std::string, String, str or nothing at all, depending on the language shown. The code is shown as snippets without a main function. Run turns the program into JavaScript with the same meaning, ignores the types, and stops loops after 1,000 rounds.
apps.question: Does it work without visible blocks?

apps.name: Level Up
apps.description: One language, Python, at every level: the toolbox grows from print and values to variables, decisions, loops and functions, and Run shows what the program prints.
apps.details:
A staircase of five levels runs across the top: Output, Variables and math, Decisions, Loops and Functions. Every level keeps the blocks of the levels before it and adds its own, so the toolbox grows with the learner while the language on the blocks stays Python all the way. The newest group of blocks is marked and scrolled into view.

Going back down a level removes the blocks that level does not have yet. A small dialog says how many blocks will go and offers Cancel, Continue and a checkbox to stop asking for the rest of the session.

The Output pane shows what the program prints as soon as it loads, and Run refreshes it. A behaviors file turns each block into JavaScript with the same meaning as its Python: range counts from 0, True and False print as in Python, 10 / 2 prints 5.0, and mistakes show up with Python's error names. Loops stop after 1,000 rounds.
apps.question: Can the toolbox grow with the learner?

apps.name: Accessible Blocks
apps.description: The same program as symbols, plain words or Java, with settings for text size, a dark theme, high contrast, a font for dyslexia and explanations on every block.
apps.details:
Symbols, Words and Java are modes: they change what a block says. Each level comes as a preset, and a twin preset adds a short explanation under every block in the toolbox. Dropdowns store one value and show it per mode, so the same choice reads "is more than" in words and > in Java. Next to the blocks, a read only view shows the same program in Java, or in plain words when the blocks are Java.

The settings change how everything looks, not what it says: a text size slider (CSS and Blockly's zoom), a dark theme, high contrast with outlined blocks, and OpenDyslexic, served by the app itself. The block colors stay apart for colorblind people, and every block also says in words what it does. Run shows what the program prints and stops loops after 1,000 rounds.
apps.question: Can blocks adapt to how people see and read?

apps.name: Many Languages
apps.description: The same twelve blocks speak English, Deutsch, Español, Ελληνικά, 中文 and العربية: pick a language and the blocks, the toolbox and the pseudocode change while the program stays.
apps.details:
Every block has a title and its text in six languages. Each language is one mode that a preset gives to the toolbox, the workspace and the pseudocode preview, so a switch shows Latin, Greek, Chinese and Arabic script and each language's own quote marks. Dropdown words such as wahr, αληθές, 真 or و come from the per element display map while the stored value stays the same; symbols such as × and ≠ are the stored values themselves.

Arabic turns the blocks, the toolbox tiles and the text right to left while the page layout stays where it is: the host decides where each view sits, the content follows the language. Blockly reads the direction only when it starts, so the app mounts the engine again and carries the program over with serializeWorkspace and loadWorkspace. The page text follows the language too, and Run shows that the program prints the same in every language.
apps.question: Can the same blocks speak the learner's language?

apps.name: Query Builder
apps.description: Blocks build a database query over a small table of planets and the text view shows it as real SQL, while Run quietly executes JavaScript with the same meaning and shows the rows as a table.
apps.details:
Eleven blocks cover a query, column picks, conditions (compare a number, compare a text, starts with, and/or) and the clauses WHERE, ORDER BY and LIMIT. The blocks read either as plain words ("only rows where moons is above 1") or as SQL, and the text view always shows the SQL. Dropdowns store one value but show it per element, so the same choice reads "is" in words, = in SQL and === in JavaScript. Connection checks let the clauses fit only in SQL's order.

Nothing here runs SQL. Behaviors turn every block into JavaScript that copies, filters, sorts and cuts a plain array of planets, and the app hands that array in and draws the rows as a results grid. A second tab shows the JavaScript that actually runs: the language on screen does not have to be the one that executes.
apps.question: Can blocks write something other than a program?
